Two-way fixed effects with an interaction, for counts of offences

Source: R/envc.R
fepnl.Rd

The regression Duan et al. (2026, eqs 6-8, pp. 9-11) use to check the drivers of recorded pollution crimes: the count on continuous drivers and the product of two of them, with unit and period fixed effects, errors clustered by unit, standardised coefficients, variance inflation factors, the simple slopes of one driver at values of the other (p. 23), and the Jarque-Bera test of the residuals (p. 25).

Usage

fepnl(
  y,
  x,
  unit,
  time,
  int = NULL,
  clus = NULL,
  at = NULL,
  ssc = "cr1",
  level = 0.95
)

# S3 method for class 'fepnl'
plot(x, ..., main = NULL, col = NULL, pal = NULL)

Arguments

y

The outcome of each row: finite numbers.

x

The drivers: a numeric matrix or data frame, one row per row of y (or one vector); column names name the terms. For plot(), a fepnl result.

unit

The unit of each row: labels.

time

The period of each row: numbers; each unit at most once per period.

int

NULL or the names of two columns of x whose product is added: the slopes are those of the first at values of the second.

clus

NULL (cluster by unit) or the cluster of each row (labels).

at

NULL or the values of int[2] for the simple slopes.

ssc

"cr1" or "none": the small-sample factor of the variance.

level

The confidence level of the intervals.

...

Passed to the base-graphics call.

main

NULL (a default title) or one string.

col

NULL (the palette) or colours.

pal

NULL (the session palette, see plotopt()) or a palette name for blpal().

Value

An object of class fepnl, a list: coef, one row per term (term, est, se, lo, hi, t, p, beta, vif); slopes (at, slope, se, lo, hi, t, p), NULL without int; fit, one row: n, units, periods, ncl (G), k (K), r2, r2w, rss; jb, a named vector skew, kurt, jb, p; vcov; resid, the residuals in the order of the rows; ssc; and level.

Details

The model is y_it = sum_j b_j x_itj + a_i + m_t + e_it, fitted by least squares after the within transformation (the kernel of didfe(), so an unbalanced panel is fine); with int = c("a", "b") the column a:b, the product of a and b, is added to x. The variance is CR1 by clus (G / (G - 1) (n - 1) / (n - K) times the sandwich, as in didfe()); ssc = "none" drops the factor. Duan et al. fitted the model with the 'linearmodels' PanelOLS estimator clustered by province and do not state its small-sample factor. Tests and intervals use Student's t on G - 1 degrees of freedom.

beta is the standardised coefficient b SD_x / SD_y of Duan et al.'s step 4 (p. 11), with the standard deviations of the columns as given (the interaction column for its term). vif is the variance inflation factor 1 / (1 - R2_j) of each column of x (with the interaction) regressed on a constant and the others over the rows used; Duan et al. drop drivers with a VIF above 10 before the fit (p. 10) and do not say whether their VIFs were pooled, as here, or within. The simple slope of int[1] at a value m of int[2] is b_a + b_ab m with variance V_aa + m^2 V_ab,ab + 2 m V_a,ab; by default at the mean and the mean plus and minus one standard deviation of int[2], Duan et al.'s points. r2 is 1 - RSS / TSS of the full model (unit and period effects counted as fitted), r2w the within R-squared. The Jarque-Bera statistic is n / 6 (S^2 + (K - 3)^2 / 4) of the residuals, with moments divided by n, on two degrees of freedom.

Duan et al.'s model is linear in a count. For a Poisson or negative binomial model with the same effects see didfe() (binary treatment) and cntreg(); Andreatta et al. (2023) fit a dynamic panel of the logged rate by system GMM, as gmmpnl() does. Melhim (2026) fits the annual crime rate of ten US states (2000-2022) on PM2.5, poverty and unemployment by pooled least squares and then with state and year fixed effects and errors clustered by state, the model here without int; the estimate changes from insignificant to positive once the state effects enter.

The plot draws the coefficients with their intervals and, with an interaction, the simple slopes at each value of the moderator; it returns what it drew.

References

Duan, H., Nie, C., He, B., Chen, X., Duan, Z., Chen, S., Song, J. and Gao, Z. (2026). A multi-method framework for decoding the spatiotemporal patterns and driving factors of environmental pollution crimes in China. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications. doi:10.1057/s41599-026-08766-9

Andreatta, D., Favarin, S., Lisciandra, M. and Millemaci, E. (2023). Digging into waste: an analysis of waste crime in the Italian provinces. Regional Studies, 57(7), 1367-1379. doi:10.1080/00343404.2022.2135697

Melhim, S. (2026). From air quality to public safety: rethinking crime dynamics and social costs of pollution in the United States. Journal of Environmental Health, 89(3), 18-25. doi:10.70387/001c.171786

Examples

# 30 provinces over 8 years: cases on the case rate, the unemployment
# rate and their product, simulated
set.seed(2)
d <- expand.grid(year = 2016:2023, prov = paste0("p", 1:30))
d$cper <- runif(240, 0.005, 0.04)
d$ur <- runif(240, 0.01, 0.03)
d$eipa <- rnorm(240, 5)
d$cases <- 50 + 9000 * d$cper + 1500 * d$ur - 4e5 * d$cper * d$ur +
  rnorm(240, sd = 5)
r <- fepnl(d$cases, d[c("cper", "eipa", "ur")], d$prov, d$year,
           int = c("cper", "ur"))
r
